guard: The same program on the walker and on the engine produces the same value, the same log, the same refusal, and the same journal entry for entry - the step keys AND their order. (FAIL-FAST suite: markers are upstream of the cells they guard.)

mutations.name: a binary expression evaluates its right operand first, so two effects journal in the wrong order
mutations.expectRed: identical on both engines: two effects in one binary expression
mutations.cell: identical on both engines: two effects in one binary expression
mutations.note: The value is 2 whichever operand ran first, so nothing about the OUTPUT notices. What notices is the journal: a step key's occurrence is allocated where the effect is reached, so swapping the operands swaps two entries and a resumed run replays into the wrong one.

mutations.name: an argument list is evaluated right to left, so two effects journal in the wrong order
mutations.expectRed: identical on both engines: two effects in one argument list
mutations.cell: identical on both engines: two effects in one argument list
mutations.note: An argument list has no emitter choice about ORDER - JavaScript evaluates the emitted expression left to right - so the mutation that breaks it is one that reorders the emission. A first attempt reversed the map and reversed it back, which restores every position AND every emitted string: it survived, correctly, because it changed nothing.

mutations.name: a member read is emitted as a native index, so the host prototype is reachable on the engine
mutations.expectRed: identical on both engines: refusals: a prototype member of a string
mutations.cell: identical on both engines: refusals: a prototype member of a string
mutations.note: A record has NO prototype to reach - `o.constructor` is undefined on both arms - so the cell that catches this is a string's, whose curated table refuses the name L4020. A native index answers the host String constructor there, which is a live capability inside a program that is supposed to have none.

mutations.name: a member WRITE is emitted as a native index, so the write path's own refusals stop happening
mutations.expectRed: identical on both engines: refusals: a curated key on the write path
mutations.cell: identical on both engines: refusals: a curated key on the write path
mutations.note: The mirror of the read mutant above. A native write silently succeeds where the walker refuses: `__proto__` reaches the real prototype and a member onto a string is dropped on the floor. Measured before it was aimed: with the write native, these two corpus programs are the first to red, and the callable-then divergences below red with them.

mutations.name: a catch binds the raw thrown value, so a program reads a different error record
mutations.expectRed: identical on both engines: catching what a refusal throws
mutations.cell: identical on both engines: catching what a refusal throws
mutations.note: `__ctx.caught` rethrows the six classes no program may catch and otherwise hands the walker's frozen {code, kind, message}. `e.code` reads the same either way, which is why this survived until a program logged the WHOLE value: raw, the engine hands back {code, name} - a different record, and one carrying a host class name.

mutations.name: a spread iterates natively, so a record stops being refused
mutations.find: return el.type === "SpreadElement" ? `...${this.seam("iter", this.expr(el.argument as AnyNode))}` : this.expr(el);
mutations.expectRed: identical on both engines: refusals: not iterable
mutations.cell: identical on both engines: refusals: not iterable
mutations.note: L4015 says arrays and strings and nothing else. A native spread of a record throws a host TypeError instead, which is a different class the program cannot catch the same way.

mutations.name: an object literal's properties are emitted in reverse, so two effects journal backwards
mutations.expectRed: identical on both engines: two effects in one object literal
mutations.cell: identical on both engines: two effects in one object literal
mutations.note: A record's own key order is observable through `keys`, `entries` and `json.stringify`, and the order its property values were EVALUATED in is observable only in the journal. This moves both.

mutations.name: a template's interpolations are emitted in reverse, so two effects journal backwards
mutations.expectRed: identical on both engines: two effects in one template
mutations.cell: identical on both engines: two effects in one template
mutations.note: Interpolation is the seam's law, but WHICH value goes into which hole, and in what order the holes were evaluated, is the transform's.

mutations.name: an array literal's elements are emitted in reverse
mutations.expectRed: identical on both engines: two effects in one array literal
mutations.cell: identical on both engines: two effects in one array literal
mutations.note: The third of the three literal positions where two effects can sit side by side.

mutations.name: a corpus program refuses before it reaches its subject, and the gate calls it identical
mutations.find: ["curated methods", 'const xs = [3, 1, 2]; log(xs.map((x) => x + 1), sort(xs), "AB".toLowerCase(), "a,b".split(","), (2.6).toFixed(1), json.stringify({ a: 1 }));', {}],
mutations.replace: ["curated methods", 'const xs = [3, 1, 2]; log(xs.map((x) => x + 1), sort(xs), "AB".lower(), (2.6).round(), json.stringify({ a: 1 }));', {}],
mutations.expectRed: every corpus program completes, or refuses the code it declares
mutations.cell: every corpus program completes, or refuses the code it declares
mutations.note: The defect this cell was written for, restored: `lower` and `round` are free builtins and not method names, so the program refuses L4014 on BOTH arms before its first log. `identical on both engines` stays green - two arms agreeing on a refusal neither program was written to produce - which is exactly how the string and number tables came to have no passing cell. This is a fixture-discipline cell, so its mutant is in the fixture.

mutations.name: a scope body evaluated at the call, so its effects journal outside the scope
mutations.find: const defers = spec !== undefined && spec.opensScope && spec.optionsAt === 2;
mutations.expectRed: identical on both engines: a fan-out whose body is awaited
mutations.cell: identical on both engines: a fan-out whose body is awaited
mutations.note: The behavioural half of the same rule: both arms journal `fanOut:f` BEFORE the `sleep` inside the body, because the body is evaluated inside the scope. Evaluated at the call, the engine journals the sleep first - a journal the walker's run never wrote, which a resume would then replay against.

mutations.name: the options bag is deferred along with the body, so the key is computed inside the scope
mutations.expectRed: identical on both engines: a fan-out whose key is awaited
mutations.cell: identical on both engines: a fan-out whose key is awaited
mutations.note: The mirror of the rule above: `sleep:warm` lands BEFORE `fanOut:f` on both arms because the options bag is evaluated at the call, outside the scope. Wrapped in a thunk it is computed inside, and the two entries swap. The ruled position is the BODY alone, so this mutant keeps every eager-body program green and shows up only as journal order in the program whose key awaits.

mutations.name: a primitive is spelled in a corpus program the run never reaches, so a kind is covered on paper
mutations.expectRed: and a corpus program journals every kind the engine can write
mutations.cell: and a corpus program journals every kind the engine can write
mutations.note: A coverage-discipline cell, so its mutant is in the fixture. The name is still SPELLED, so the free-name cell stays green and both arms still agree; only a kind the engine actually wrote to a journal counts here, and `monitor` stops being one. Measured before it was aimed: this is the only cell that reds.

mutations.name: the dead-zone rule never looks at writes, so an early write dies as a native ReferenceError
mutations.expectRed: identical on both engines: a dead-zone write
mutations.cell: identical on both engines: a dead-zone write
mutations.note: The behavioural half of the surface cell: the walker answers a CATCHABLE L2004 and the program still reads the declared value afterwards, where the mutant's engine dies on an engine fault the program cannot see. Measured before it was aimed.

mutations.name: the survival list points at a corpus row that completes, so the check is a comment
mutations.find: ["issue 642 through the set door: a callable then, then any later reference to the record", "refusals: a callable then, then a later reference to the record"],
mutations.replace: ["issue 642 through the set door: a callable then, then any later reference to the record", "absence and NaN are data, and still log"],
mutations.expectRed: the oracle's own process survives it, and hands the refusal back to its caller: issue 642 through the set door
mutations.cell: the oracle's own process survives it, and hands the refusal back to its caller: issue 642 through the set door: a callable then, then any later reference to the record
mutations.note: Surviving is not the claim; coming back as the ruled refusal is. Point the entry at a corpus row that COMPLETES and the child prints COMPLETED with exit 0 - the lookup still finds a row, the process still survives, and a check reading only the exit code would stay green over a section that had stopped measuring the value law at all.

mutations.name: the survival list names a corpus row that is gone, so it checks a program the gate no longer runs
mutations.find: ["issue 642 through the set door: a callable then, then any later reference to the record", "refusals: a callable then, then a later reference to the record"],
mutations.replace: ["issue 642 through the set door: a callable then, then any later reference to the record", "refusals: a callable then written onto a rekord"],
mutations.expectRed: the survival check names a corpus row that still exists, so the two cannot drift apart: issue 642 through the set door
mutations.cell: the survival check names a corpus row that still exists, so the two cannot drift apart: issue 642 through the set door: a callable then, then any later reference to the record
mutations.note: This list held its programs as LITERALS until now - two copies of each source with nothing keeping them equal, on the one section whose job is to stop those rows hanging the suite, so a drift would have been silent and green. The programs live in the corpus and are looked up by name, which removes text drift entirely; what remains is a row that is renamed or deleted out from under the reference, and that is what this mutant is. Note what it does NOT grade, since the lookup only asks whether A row was found: pointing the entry at a DIFFERENT row that exists passes this cell, and is caught by the mutant above it only because that row completes.

mutations.name: the child swallows a failure that escaped the caller, so an uncatchable refusal reads as a caught one
mutations.expectRed: the oracle's own process survives it, and hands the refusal back to its caller: issue 642 through the set door
mutations.cell: the oracle's own process survives it, and hands the refusal back to its caller: issue 642 through the set door: a callable then, then any later reference to the record
mutations.note: The OTHER clause, and the one the whole section exists for. These three used to fail in ways a corpus row cannot report - one killed the interpreter's process outright, two never settled - so what the cell has to notice is a refusal that does NOT come back catchable. Break the child's catch and the failure escapes exactly as it used to: the process dies, nothing is printed, and the cell reds on the exit code. Without this mutant the survival clause is graded by nothing, because no program left in the language still kills the oracle.

mutations.name: `undefined` is emitted as the global name, so a module the gate runs is no longer closed
mutations.expectRed: every corpus program emits a module with no free identifier, which is what the compartment cannot catch
mutations.cell: every corpus program emits a module with no free identifier, which is what the compartment cannot catch
mutations.note: Measured: NOT ONE behavioural cell in this suite reds. The free name resolves to the real global in the harness's evaluator, and lane H measured that inside the shipped SES compartment an unbound READ answers `undefined` and throws nothing either - so both arms agree, every journal matches, and the only thing that notices is the resolver over the emitted text. That is the whole argument for running it over the corpus this gate actually executes.

mutations.name: the shape leg is never compared, so the gate is back to comparing renderings
mutations.expectRed: the comparator finds a difference the rendering cannot show: absence against a literal null
mutations.cell: the comparator finds a difference the rendering cannot show: absence against a literal null
mutations.note: A comparator-discipline cell, so its mutant is in the comparator. Every corpus row still passes without this leg - that is the whole point, the blindness was latent - so only the hand-built pairs notice, which is what makes them the evidence that the leg can fail at all.

mutations.name: the shape signature goes shallow, so a record carrying a function reads as an empty one
mutations.expectRed: the comparator finds a difference the rendering cannot show: an empty record against one carrying a function
mutations.cell: the comparator finds a difference the rendering cannot show: an empty record against one carrying a function, which is the nesting a shallow signature missed
mutations.note: The first spelling of this signature WAS shallow, and lane H measured that it failed the two rows it had been added for: `{ g: (x) => x }` and `{}` both read `object`, and it is the NESTED closure rather than the bare one that killed the worker with a DataCloneError. The top-level pairs still pass shallow, so only the nesting controls red.

mutations.name: negative zero loses its sign in the signature, so `0 / -1` reads as zero
mutations.expectRed: the comparator finds a difference the rendering cannot show: zero against negative zero
mutations.cell: the comparator finds a difference the rendering cannot show: zero against negative zero, which `0 / -1` produces in an ordinary program
mutations.note: Lane H's second hole in the first spelling. JSON draws -0 as `0` and so does a bare `typeof`, and `0 / -1`, `-0` and `0 * -1` are three ordinary programs that produce a true one, measured on both arms - they are corpus rows now, so this bit has live evidence and not only a control.
